rv.q: The production is a wonderful achievement.
Ferran and Thallon have a brilliantly natural chemistry, warmly charting the familiar steps from cringingly awkward flirtations through growing intimacy to volatile first love.

Wohl's sensitively wrought play is not an apology for fascism, saying all Nazis are just mixed-up kids. But it is a drama about radicalisation, about two lonely teenagers who don't know how they feel about the world, being exposed to a monolithically certain belief system.
The writing never quite delivers on the promise of its arrestingly grotesque set-up.
The storytelling is ingenious and well-paced, and the depth and subtlety of the characters provide constant surprises.
A stealthily powerful play gets the production of its dreams in Camp Siegfried.
While the plotting seems a little contrived, there is both point and poignancy in the writing and this is matched in the vibrant performances of Luke Thallon and Patsy Ferran as the young couple.
Ultimately, despite its many felicities, as the evening progresses you realize you're never in doubt about what the author wants you to think.
The play is however served by a nigh-on faultless production.
The play is 90 minutes long (without a break) and although it is a series of exchanges between Him and Her, it never drags.
Although the characters' motivations do not always convince, the performances are top notch.
Camp Siegfried is 1 of the most outstanding pieces of new writing we've seen this year and it's absolutely thrilling to see it brought to life by such a talented young acting pairing.

cn.t: Critics laud this production as a "wonderful achievement," praising its extraordinary use of space and purposeful Trump-era political resonances in depicting 1930s German-American culture and the rise of fascism.
